Keeping with tradition, newly discovered elements can be named after: (a) a mythological concept or character (including an astronomical object), (b) a mineral or similar substance, (c) a place, or geographical region, (d) a property of the element, or (e) a scientist.

One of these things is not like the others. (hint: the one that is painfully arbitrary.)

I have no idea which of these you think is more arbitrary than the others. They are all pretty well represented in existing elements for not-insane reasons. Examples:

  • Helium - Helios the sun god because it was discovered in the atmosphere of the sun.
  • Beryllium - Beryl, a mineral that contains it.
  • Ytterbium -Ytterby, the location of a mine which produced rocks in which the element was found.
  • Chromium - "Chroma" which means "color" referring to the many different colors of salts it forms.
  • Curium - Marie and Pierre Curie, the couple that discovered radium and performed significant early research on radioactivity.

If anything, the first and the last are the weirdest, but neither is "arbitrary". It's not like the researchers that name the elements pick the names out of a hat: The names are still significant.

Doesn't naming something that is scientifically factual after a make-believe concept unnecessarily muddle the lines between fact and fiction? Science should not be using mythological concepts or characters for naming something that is discovered in reality.

nihonium, Nh : for Nihon, a Japanese word for Japan

muscovium, Mc : for Moscow

tennessine, Ts : for Tennessee

oganesson, Og: for professor Yuri Oganessian, recognizing "His pioneering contributions to transactinoid elements research."

Here is what I said in response to a similar question that was asked awhile ago.

Attorney here.

It is possible to represent oneself in traffic court, small claims, even probate depending on the complexity of the estate. However, beyond that, with no training, you are going to find yourself very quickly out of your element. There is a lot of procedure to court. Things just have to be done a certain way. Yes there are overarching rules that apply to all the courts, but there are also a bunch of little variances between jurisdictions. Thus, without familiarity with those procedures, you are going to have a very difficult time trying to make headway against an experienced attorney on the other side. Plus, you are most likely not going to be familiar with the judge, an experienced attorney will be. That attorney is going to know what that judge likes, doesn't like, and how to use that to his advantage.

Having said all that, it simply comes down to the fact that you are emotionally invested in the case. Even if one is an attorney, representing oneself is a bad idea. You are focused on seeing your side of the case, and it is very difficult to extract yourself from that. You need someone who will advocate for you, but can also keep a clear head about what the other side has going for/against it. Many people are convinced their case is black and white. It rarely is. It is almost always some shade of grey, and that's why you need somebody who can look at the whole picture.

You forgot to mention half the lower court judges are political appointees / hacks or elected due to connections and pull rather than merit and legal knowledge. So even if you were very smart and capable in the law, be prepared to appeal because your lower court judges often times don't like your tie and you will lose, and especially dont like your tie when you dont have an attorney representing you, even where you are totally right on the law.

Welcome to justice American style.
